etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin articulātus (“distinct, articulated, jointed”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

definitions.definition: Speaking in a clear and effective manner.
Consisting of segments united by joints.
(obsolete) Expressed in articles or in separate items or particulars.

quote.citation: 1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “II. Century.”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC:

definitions.definition: (obsolete, of sound) Related to human speech, as distinct from the vocalisation of animals.

quote.citation: 1728, James Knapton, John Knapton, Cyclopaedia, or an Universal Dictionary of Arts and Sciences, page 146:
quote.text: Brutes cannot form articulate Sounds, cannot articulate the Sounds of the Voice, excepting some few Birds, as the Parrot, Pye, &c.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From a substantivation of the above adjective through the associated taxon's name, Articulata (see -ate (noun-forming suffix)).

definitions.definition: (zoology) An animal of the subkingdom Articulata.

quote.citation: 1977, Bulletin of the British Museum (Natural History):
quote.text: They considered articulates to be pre-adapted for an eleutherozoic existence because they possess muscular arms which are potentially of value in crawling and swimming, as in comatulids.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From the adjective, see the etymology at -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To speak clearly; to enunciate.
(transitive) To explain; to put into words; to make something specific.
(transitive) To bend or hinge something at intervals, or to allow or build something so that it can bend.
(music, transitive) to attack a note, as by tonguing, slurring, bowing, etc.
(anatomy, intransitive) to form a joint or connect by joints

quote.citation: c. 1605–1608, William Shakespeare, Coriolanus, act 1, scene 9, lines 75–77:
quote.text: Send us to Rome / The best, with whom we may articulate / For their own good and ours.
